title: 7 Days of Real-World Learning
tagline: One activity a day. Done together. Zero worksheets.

photo.alt: A boy and his younger sister choosing a loaf of bread together in a grocery store
photo.caption: Day 2: $40, a grocery store, and dinner is their call.

paras: I'm the mom behind Anywhere Learning. The skills kids need most don't come from textbooks. They come from real life: counting the change at a checkout, pricing cookies for a stand, telling a story at dinner that makes everyone lean in.

These 7 activities are ones we've done ourselves. Each one mixes real math, writing or science with a life skill, inside something you actually do together. Most fit into an hour or two, with what's already at home:

list.v: making a tough call and standing by it
planning an event for someone else

letter.close: No need to follow the order or do all seven. Pick the one that fits today, and do it together.
letter.pull: This is what learning looks like when real life does the teaching.

howto.intro: Every day works the same way: four moves you do together, and three levels so it fits your kid.

tips.title: You do it with them
tips.text: Your part is small but it matters: set it up, ask, play along, then let them make the calls.

tips.title: Starting points, not scripts
tips.text: If your kid takes it somewhere unexpected, follow them. The best moments are the ones you didn't plan.

tips.title: Pick the level
tips.text: Explore, Develop or Extend: choose what fits today. Siblings can each do their own.

tips.title: Ask, then wait
tips.text: The best answers come after the pause, often later at dinner or in the car.

tips.title: Low prep is the point
tips.text: If it starts to feel like work, stop and come back another day.

tips.title: Use it again
tips.text: A land art piece in spring is a new activity in fall. Keep this guide and come back to it.

days.title: Land Art Challenge
days.caption: My daughter's inukshuk family, with a story for each one.
days.why: No art lessons and no supplies: whatever nature leaves on the ground becomes the material.
days.need: Fallen leaves, sticks, rocks, pinecones or petals, and a phone for photos
together: Your kid picks a challenge: a mandala using 4 different natural materials, the tallest tower of loose stones, or art that shows a feeling.
They gather only fallen things: nothing alive, nothing from an animal's home, and towers away from trails and water.
They build it while you stay close and curious. Then you ask for a title and the story behind it, instead of just 'beautiful'.
Photograph it, then put every piece back where it came from.

levels.develop: Add a twist: one material only, or twice the size.
levels.extend: Title it, and explain one choice you made and why.

days.skill: Making art from what's on the ground
days.learn: Patterns, symmetry and shapes, plus observation and leaving no trace

next.v: six crafts from what's on the ground, like soil paint and a wind chime tuned by ear

days.title: The $20 Snack Mission
days.time: About an hour, plus the store
days.caption: Choosing the bread, with $40 for the whole meal.
days.why: A real budget in a real store turns adding, rounding and trade-offs into math kids actually want to get right.
days.need: $20 in cash (any amount works), paper and a pencil, and any grocery or corner store
together: You set a real mission, like snacks for the week or a movie night, and the budget. Say it once: whatever is left, they keep.
Your kid writes the list and guesses each price before you go. Wrong guesses are part of it.
In the store, they round each price up and keep a running total. You walk beside them and let them do the adding.
When the total bumps the budget, they choose what goes back, and you ask why that one. Then they pay and count the change.

levels.explore: Pick two or three things and check each one fits the budget before it goes in the basket.
levels.develop: Keep the running total on your own and finish under budget.
levels.extend: Is '2 for $5' cheaper than $2.29 each? Work it out at the shelf.

days.learn: Adding, rounding, estimating and unit prices, plus making trade-offs

next.v: a real budget at a market, unit prices stall to stall, and a meal planned from what's in season

days.title: Invent a Sport
days.caption: Get Blocked: their own trampoline sport.
days.why: Inventing a game nobody has played means designing a field, rules and a fair way to win, then watching it break and fixing it.
days.need: A ball (rolled-up socks indoors), shoes or buckets as markers, and chalk or painter's tape
together: Your kid picks how you win: hit a target, race, capture something or last the longest. They try the idea with a ball for two minutes first.
They mark a start, a goal and the edges. You check the space together: no glass, no stairs, no hard corners.
They say the rules out loud, with one way to score. You find the gaps: 'What if two people grab it at once?'
Everyone plays a round. Play for real, no fake-losing. Then they change one rule and play again.

levels.explore: Pick how you win, mark the field and play one round.
levels.develop: Name the sport, write the rules down and fix two things after the first round.
levels.extend: Play 6 games, swapping who starts. If whoever starts wins most, change the start and test again.

days.learn: Scoring, distances and clear written rules, plus design thinking and movement

next.v: a board game invented from nothing, then handed to someone new to see what breaks

days.title: What Would You Do?
days.caption: One question, on the way somewhere.
days.why: Tough little decisions with no easy answer build the thinking kids need when nobody's there to tell them what's right.
days.need: Nothing at all. The car, a walk or dinner works best.
together: Read out a situation: 'The clerk gave you too much change, and nobody would know.' Everyone says their gut answer at the same time.
Your kid finds every way out of it: the obvious one, the safe one, the brave one and the one nobody's said yet.
For each option, they work out who's glad, who's upset and what happens next. You keep asking: who's on the other side of this?
They choose and say why. Then you push back the way a friend would, and they decide again.

levels.explore: Find two options, with one good and one bad thing about each.
levels.develop: Find three or four options, including one nobody expected, and who each one affects.
levels.extend: Compare tomorrow with a year from now for each option, then rank them and defend the order.

days.full: What Would You Do? Decision Lab
days.learn: Explaining and defending a choice, plus fairness and empathy

next.v: a real debate with research, a timer, a judge and a verdict

days.title: The Two-Minute Story
days.caption: Two stories, two minutes each, told at the kitchen counter.
days.why: Telling one real moment clearly, in about two minutes, is how we make friends and hold a room. Every kid already has the stories.
days.need: A timer (a phone works). That's it.
together: Play two truths and a lie as a family, and notice which stories sounded true, and why.
Your kid picks one true moment from their life. Not 'my whole trip': one small moment.
You listen once without interrupting, then ask: where were you, what changed, and why does it matter?
They tell it again with a timer running, cut what the story doesn't need, and tell it for real at dinner.

levels.explore: Tell a true moment with a clear beginning and end.
levels.develop: Find the beginning, the turn and the point, and get it to about two minutes.
levels.extend: Cut it to 60 seconds, then add back only what you missed.

days.learn: Story structure and speaking out loud, plus confidence

next.v: an interview with someone in your community, turned into a profile others want to read

days.title: Pricing Experiment
days.caption: $1 a cookie, or buy four, get one free.
days.why: Most kids guess a price. Testing two prices with real buyers teaches cost, profit and what people value.
days.need: Something to sell, like cookies or lemonade, the supply receipt, a place to sell and paper for a tally
together: Your kid works out what one costs to make from the receipt. You help with the math and ask what they nearly forgot, like cups or bags.
They pick two prices above that cost, a lower one and a higher one, and predict which will earn more.
They sell for an hour at each price, in the same spot, keeping a tally. You stay close, and check your local rules for selling homemade food.
They count what they kept at each price. You ask: more sales, or more money? Then they choose the price their numbers support.

levels.explore: Pick a low and a high price, and count how many sell at each.
levels.develop: Tally sales, money in and money kept at both prices, then compare.
levels.extend: Work out how many you'd need to sell just to cover the supplies.

days.learn: Cost of one, profit and a fair test, plus what buyers will pay

next.v: a tiny business that keeps going for weeks, with every cost and sale tracked

days.title: Scavenger Hunt Designer
days.caption: The rockstar host, reading the next riddle.
days.why: Designing a hunt for someone else means thinking like a player: where they'll look, what they'll miss and how long it takes.
days.need: A yard, a park or the house, paper and a pencil, and at least one player who isn't the designer
together: Your kid picks a theme, who's playing and the prize at the finish.
You walk the space together and set the boundaries: no roads, nothing to climb. They pick five hiding spots inside them.
They write or draw a clue for each spot that leads to the next. You read each one as a newcomer would, and say so if you'd be stuck.
They hide the clues and run the hunt: the welcome, the hints, the prize. Play to win, then ask what they'd change.

levels.explore: Five spots and five clues, written or drawn.
levels.develop: Eight spots and at least two kinds of clue, tested before the hunt.
levels.extend: Ten clues that get harder, including one code players have to crack.

days.learn: Writing riddles, mapping a route and timing, plus planning an event

next.v: real codes to make and crack, including one with no key at all

finish.headline: You just did the hard part.
finish.text: If you did even one of these days, you stepped in beside your kid and let real life do the teaching. That's the whole thing.
finish.quote: The families raising curious, capable kids aren't the ones who found the perfect workbook. They're the ones who said yes to the real-world stuff, again and again.
finish.fullText: Each day is the short version of a full guide in the membership, with step-by-step help, a toolkit and three levels for ages 6 to 14. There are 120+ guides in all.
finish.cta: Come see what's inside. Free for 7 days.
